passage: The placement hall at the engineering college was packed with final-year students queuing at the bank-exam coaching stall. Pankaj stood at the other end, near the small table of a design studio, with his phone buzzing: Papa, again. Around him, batchmates drifted toward the crowd one after another. Elizabeth, who had already signed up for the studio's portfolio round, glanced at him. “Coming?” she asked. Pankaj thought of his father's voice at dinner: “A government post is security.” He also thought of the sketchbook in his bag. He folded the studio's form into his pocket without filling it, then walked slowly to the end of the long queue. The coaching counsellor handed him a token, smiling.

qa.q: What did Pankaj fold into his pocket?
qa.a: He folded the studio's form into his pocket without filling it.

qa.q: What does Pankaj feel torn between as he stands at the design studio table?
qa.a: Pankaj is torn between his father's wish for the security of a government post and his own pull toward design. The buzzing phone and the sketchbook in his bag show both.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do to work through this without cutting either side off?
qa.a: He could talk honestly with his father about the design interest, perhaps after the studio's portfolio round, and ask a counsellor to help him look at both paths.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth see Pankaj's hesitation?
qa.a: Elizabeth may see that he wants the studio path but something holds him back, since she invited him with “Coming?” and glanced at him.

grounding: A young adult feels the duty of family expectations about career and a wish for his own path, and follows the crowd for now.

Dear Baljeet,
You asked how the visit went. Fine, on the surface. Papa read out the list of rishtas while Mummy poured tea and Dadi nodded, and I said, “Let me finish the training first.” Chachi said, “A girl's time is short.” Uncle changed the subject. My cousin Ria stared into her cup. I'm not angry at them, they truly want me settled. But part of me is furious that no one asked what I want, and part of me wants to be the child they hoped for. I told them I'd think. I don't know yet which one I'm thinking for.
Mridul

qa.q: What is Mridul feeling about the family's expectations?
qa.a: Mridul feels loyal and resentful at once: not angry at the family who want Mridul settled, yet furious that no one asked what Mridul wants.

qa.q: What could Mridul do before giving the family an answer?
qa.a: Mridul could decide what matters most and talk it through with one trusted relative, then give the family a clear, kind reply about timing.

qa.q: How might Chachi see her own comment?
qa.a: Chachi probably sees it as practical care about time passing, while it lands on Mridul as pressure.

passage:
Dear Sonali,
Remember how we joked at school that I'd end up running Abbu's pharmacy? It's happening. At Eid, the whole family sat around the dastarkhwan, and my uncles took turns telling me how lucky I am to have a ready business. Ammi looked so hopeful. My younger sister kept kicking me under the cloth, because she knows about the sound-engineering course I got into in Pune.
I didn't say anything. I love them, and I know Abbu built that shop from nothing. But I also felt this hot, angry thing in my chest, like my plans were furniture they could move around. Both feelings are real, and neither one goes away.
Can I call you on Sunday? I need someone who isn't family.
Tanvir

qa.q: Which course did Tanvir get into?
qa.a: The sound-engineering course in Pune.

qa.q: What two feelings is Tanvir carrying at the Eid gathering?
qa.a: Tanvir feels love and loyalty toward the family, knowing Abbu built the shop from nothing, and also anger and resentment that Tanvir's own plans are being moved around.

qa.q: What could Tanvir try before the next family conversation?
qa.a: Talk first with one parent alone, calmly explaining the course and why it matters, rather than facing all the uncles at once.

qa.q: How does Tanvir's younger sister seem to see the situation?
qa.a: She knows about the course and seems to side with Tanvir, kicking under the cloth as if urging Tanvir to speak up.

grounding: A young adult feels both loyal to the family's career plan and resentful of it, and neither feeling cancels the other.

passage: Ojas, you asked why I've been missing the fest meetings. Okay, here's the honest Jahnavi version. Every weekend there's a 'family lunch' at home, and somehow another family with a marriageable son is also there. My aunts smile, my father talks about my cooking, which is funny because I burn rice. And I sit there and smile back, because my mother has been planning this for months and she looks so pleased. I don't hate them for it. I'd like to marry someday. But I got an internship offer in Bengaluru, and when I mentioned it, my aunt said, 'After the wedding, see.' I felt so angry I had to go and splash water on my face. Then that night I massaged my mother's feet like always. That's the mess. I'm loyal and I'm furious at the same time.

qa.q: Where is Jahnavi's internship offer?
qa.a: In Bengaluru.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when the aunt said 'After the wedding, see'?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt furious, enough to go and splash water on their face, yet still felt loyal and massaged the mother's feet that night.

qa.q: What would you advise Jahnavi to do about the internship?
qa.a: Choose a calm time to talk with the mother alone, share how much the internship means and ask whether the wedding plans can wait until after it.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's mother see these weekend lunches?
qa.a: She has planned them for months and looks pleased, so she probably sees them as caring for Jahnavi's future, not as blocking it.

grounding: A young adult is pulled between family marriage plans and an internship, feeling both loyal and resentful at once.

passage: March: At dinner, Abbu announced that Afreen would start coaching for the civil services exam, like her cousin. Everyone clapped. Afreen smiled and said nothing, thinking of the design job offer from Joseph's startup sitting in her inbox. April: She went to coaching every morning and did design work for Joseph at night. On the bus she felt proud of her family's faith in her, and angry that nobody had asked. Some days she felt both before she reached her stop. May: She told Ammi first, in the kitchen. Ammi was quiet for a long time, then said, 'Show your Abbu the designs. Let him see what you're choosing.' Afreen didn't feel lighter, exactly. She still felt both things, but she had stopped hiding one of them.

qa.q: Who did Afreen tell first in May?
qa.a: She told Ammi first, in the kitchen.

qa.q: What did Afreen feel on the bus in April?
qa.a: She felt proud of her family's faith in her and angry that nobody had asked her, sometimes both on the same ride.

qa.q: Which step helped Afreen most, and why?
qa.a: Telling Ammi privately first; it gave her an ally and a plan, showing Abbu the designs, instead of hiding the job.

qa.q: What would change if Abbu had asked Afreen what she wanted back in March?
qa.a: She might not have spent April split between coaching and night work, and the family could have weighed both paths openly.

grounding: Over three months a young adult carries both loyalty to a family career plan and resentment about it, and begins to speak up.

passage:
Disha, you asked how I chose design when Papa wanted engineering. Let your Binita didi tell you honestly. It wasn't one brave moment.
At twenty I was in second-year engineering, because everyone in our family is an engineer: Papa, Chacha, Dada. I loved them. I didn't want Papa to feel his years of overtime had been wasted.
Every night I sketched dresses in the back of my circuits notebook and felt guilty, then angry that I felt guilty. Both at once, every day, for a year.
At Diwali, Chacha joked about "our future engineer", and I burst into tears in front of everyone. Later Papa found me on the terrace. I showed him the notebook. He turned the pages for a long time. He didn't say yes. He said, "Finish this year. Then we'll visit the design college together."
I still felt grateful and resentful at once, Disha. Both were true.

qa.q: Where did Binita sketch dresses?
qa.a: In the back of the circuits notebook.

qa.q: What feelings did Binita carry through that year?
qa.a: Guilt and anger at once: loyal to Papa and his hard work, yet resentful of a path she didn't choose.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Showing Papa the notebook on the terrace; it let him see her real interest, and he offered a next step instead of a flat no.

qa.q: What might Papa have felt turning the notebook pages?
qa.a: Papa probably felt surprised and torn, maybe proud of the drawings and sad he hadn't noticed sooner.

grounding: Shows a young adult torn between family expectations about career and her own path, feeling loyal and resentful at the same time.
